title: Aging Far From Home: How Indian-American Seniors Are Building Support Systems That Don't Exist in Mainstream America
excerpt: From community-run senior centres in Queens to Ayurvedic wellness retreats in California, diaspora Indians are pioneering culturally rooted approaches to aging — because the Western eldercare model was never built for them.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Indian-American seniors face unique challenges in aging due to cultural differences in eldercare.
  • Community organizations are creating culturally competent support systems for elderly South Asians.
  • The demand for culturally appropriate eldercare is growing as the Indian-American population ages.
  • Programs focus on preventing isolation and promoting health tailored to South Asian needs.
  • Culturally specific nutrition and wellness practices are essential for the aging diaspora.

When Mukund Mehta surveys the elderly South Asian faces at India Home's senior centres in Queens, New York, he sees a population that exists in a gap no American institution was designed to fill. These are parents and grandparents who moved to the United States decades ago — or were brought over on family-sponsored green cards in their sixties and seventies — who now navigate old age in a country where the food tastes wrong, the language is a barrier, and the eldercare system assumes a cultural context that is not theirs. "The isolation is the killer," Mehta said during a recent GOPIO International webinar on diaspora aging held in late June. "Not literally — though it contributes to that too. But the isolation from familiar food, familiar language, familiar social rituals. That is what erodes mental health first, and physical health follows." ## A Community Built From Scratch GOPIO International — the Global Organization of People of Indian Origin — convened its June 2026 webinar, titled "Diaspora Indians – Aging Gracefully," to spotlight the organisations and individuals building what mainstream America has not: culturally competent eldercare for South Asians. The panel brought together service providers, Ayurvedic practitioners, nutritionists, and community organisers from across the United States, each addressing a different facet of the aging diaspora's needs. Dr. Vasundhara Kalasapudi, founder of India Home in Queens, described how her organisation serves over a thousand elderly South Asians annually across multiple cultural and linguistic communities — Bengali, Hindi, Urdu, Punjabi, Gujarati. The centres offer more than meals and activities; they provide a social world where elders can speak their own language, eat their own food, and gather with people who share their cultural references. India Home's model has become a template. Operating out of community spaces in Jackson Heights, Jamaica, and Sunnyside, the organisation runs blood pressure screenings adapted for South Asian cardiovascular risk profiles, nutrition counselling that works with desi diets rather than against them, and social programming that fights the epidemic of elder isolation. ## The Five Pillars > **""When I tell a 75-year-old Gujarati grandmother to eat more protein, I cannot hand her a pamphlet about chicken breast and Greek yoghurt," Batheja said."** Preeti Singh, who directs the South Asian Senior Association (SASA) out of Irvine, California, presented a framework she calls the five pillars of aging gracefully for the diaspora: 1. **Preventing isolation** — creating social structures that replicate the extended-family support network that most first-generation immigrants left behind in India 2. **Purposeful engagement** — activities, volunteering, and intergenerational programmes that give elders a reason to leave the house 3. **Preventive care** — regular health screenings tailored to South Asian risk factors, particularly cardiovascular disease, diabetes, and hypertension 4. **Government resource navigation** — helping elders access Medicare, Medicaid, SNAP benefits, and local services they often do not know exist 5. **Planning ahead** — estate planning, advance directives, and long-term care discussions that many South Asian families avoid until crisis hits SASA's model is distinctive for its partnership with municipal governments. In cities like Irvine and Anaheim, it works directly with city recreation departments to host subsidised programmes, charging modest fees to remain self-sustaining while keeping services accessible. ## Nutrition That Respects the Palate Rita Batheja, a registered dietitian specialising in integrative and functional medicine, addressed perhaps the most personal dimension of aging in the diaspora: food. "When I tell a 75-year-old Gujarati grandmother to eat more protein, I cannot hand her a pamphlet about chicken breast and Greek yoghurt," Batheja said. "I have to talk about soy beverages she would recognise, the paneer she already eats, chickpeas, nuts and seeds, sprouted moong. The nutrition science is universal. The delivery has to be culturally specific." Batheja emphasised the role of electrolytes — sodium, potassium, magnesium, and calcium — in proper hydration for elderly South Asians, many of whom drink inadequate water due to habits carried over from a lifetime of rationed consumption. She also highlighted the importance of gut health and the microbiome, recommending a "rainbow diet" of diverse vegetables and fermented foods like dahi and pickled vegetables that South Asian cuisine already incorporates naturally.
The Five Pillars of Aging Gracefully
›Preventing isolation through social structures.
›Purposeful engagement with activities and volunteering.
›Preventive care tailored to South Asian health risks.
›Navigating government resources for elder benefits.
›Planning ahead for estate and long-term care.
## The Ayurvedic Bridge Dr. Jaya Daptardar, an Ayurvedic doctor and healthcare executive, described panchakarma — the Ayurvedic detoxification protocol — as a framework for addressing the accumulated toxins and inflammation that accelerate aging. While panchakarma is not a replacement for evidence-based Western medicine, Daptardar argued it can complement it, particularly in managing the chronic inflammation and stress-related conditions prevalent among diaspora elders. Tirlok Malik, a filmmaker and founder of Happy Life Yoga and Ayurveda Wellness, echoed this integrative approach. His retreats combine yoga, Ayurvedic nutrition, and community gathering — designed specifically for South Asian seniors who feel alienated by the mainstream yoga-studio culture of American cities. ## The Scale of the Challenge According to the Pew Research Center, Indian Americans are one of the fastest-growing demographic groups in the United States, with a population exceeding 4.8 million. As the first major wave of Indian immigrants from the 1970s and 1980s ages into their seventies and eighties, the demand for culturally appropriate eldercare is growing exponentially. Yet the supply remains thin. India Home, SASA, and a handful of other organisations serve thousands, but the need runs into hundreds of thousands. Many elderly South Asians live with adult children in suburbs with no public transit, no community centre within walking distance, and no social network outside the family. GOPIO Chairman Dr. Abraham Thomas acknowledged the gap. "We have built businesses, contributed to technology and medicine, raised families. But we have not built the infrastructure for our own aging. That is the next frontier for the diaspora."
Nutrition for South Asian Seniors
›Culturally specific nutrition is vital for health.
›Focus on familiar foods like paneer and chickpeas.
›Electrolyte balance is crucial for hydration.
›Emphasis on gut health and a diverse diet.
The organisation's next convention, scheduled for December 18-20, 2026 at the Garware Club in Mumbai, will include continued sessions on senior welfare alongside its broader agenda of diaspora advocacy. *Sources: GOPIO International webinar, "Diaspora Indians – Aging Gracefully" (June 13, 2026), The Indian EYE, Diverse Elders Coalition, India Home Inc., South Asian Senior Association (SASA)*
